title: The Tale of Agafya and the Widow of the Well
symbols: α β γ δ ε ζ A B C ↑ D E F K ↓ Pr Rs M N U

pages.text: They still tell of Agafya Last-of-Eleven in a hut beside a river that ran uphill on Sundays: the one, whom nobody remembered to name until she was six.
Then old father Foma went off to sell a cow and a silence, and Agafya was left in charge.
Before leaving, old father Foma warned Agafya: “do not answer if someone calls your name from the forest.” The girl said “Of course”, and began to wonder at once.
Forbidden things are heavy; Agafya Last-of-Eleven could not stop carrying this one.
Meanwhile the Widow of the Well came sniffing round the house, asking questions.
The goat told the stranger everything, and the Widow wrote it on a fingernail.
In the morning there was a wet place where Tsarevna Lumina had been. The Widow had come.
Old father Foma rang the cracked bell, and it was Agafya who answered.
“I have nothing better to do, and I will go,” said Agafya.
And Agafya went, it may be near, it may be far; the tale is quick, the road is not. At the crossroads stone, the girl chose the road down a ladder of roots, deeper than the wells go.
The Grandmother of Owls in a hut built entirely of locked doors held out a cracked cup: “Feed me, or pass on hungry yourself.”
Three days later Agafya found a clever answer.

The Grandmother of Owls opened a sack that held three things: a handkerchief that unfolds into a lake; a ball of red thread that knows the way; a birch-bark flute that makes the dead dance politely. The Grandmother of Owls gave our Agafya a handkerchief that unfolds into a lake.
The spell came unstitched, and Tsarevna Lumina was free.
With the prize in her cap, the girl turned for home.
The Widow scuttled on a hundred borrowed legs after Agafya, shrieking.
When the teeth were an inch away, the doll snatched Agafya up.
There was one more task: to eat a whole oven of bread before dawn.
The task was done by morning.
The Widow was made to count the crows of the kingdom, and is counting still.
